planting.note: Plant dormant culm divisions or nursery plugs directly into loose dune sand from late fall through early spring, spacing them in staggered rows to trap blowing sand; seed propagation is unreliable, so vegetative culms are the standard method.

directions: American beachgrass is the primary dune-building grass of the Atlantic Coast and Great Lakes, forming dense colonies of stiff, blue-green, rolled leaf blades from deep, cord-like rhizomes that trap wind-blown sand and raise the dune crest around them. It thrives on continual sand burial and salt spray that would smother most other plants, and actually grows more vigorously when periodically covered by fresh sand. Mature stands produce narrow, cylindrical flower spikes in summer but spread mainly by rhizome rather than seed. In many coastal states it is a legally protected species on public dunes, planted extensively in beach nourishment and storm-recovery projects but rarely grown in conventional garden beds away from the shoreline.

planting.note: Direct sow into loose, well-drained dune or beach sand in full sun after the threat of hard frost passes; plants form a low rosette the first season and typically flower the following year.

directions: Seabeach evening primrose sprawls flat across open dune sand from the mid-Atlantic south to the Gulf Coast, its silvery, hairy stems radiating out from a central rosette of narrow gray-green leaves. Large, four-petaled, pale lemon-yellow flowers open in late afternoon and through the night, fading to a soft pink-orange by the next morning, and attract night-flying moths as pollinators. It is adapted to pure, infertile beach sand and salt spray and declines quickly in rich or irrigated garden soil, making it suitable mainly for true coastal or xeric sand gardens. Established plants persist for several years as a loose, trailing groundcover on the open, sun-baked upper beach and dune front.

planting.note: Direct sow into loose, dry beach or dune sand in full sun after the soil has warmed in spring; this low annual self-sows readily in open sand and needs no transplanting.

directions: Seaside spurge is a small, prostrate annual that forms flat, reddish mats of tiny opposite leaves on the open sand of the upper beach and foredune from the Canadian Maritimes and Great Lakes south to the Gulf Coast. Its thin, wiry stems exude a milky latex sap typical of the spurge family, and inconspicuous flowers give way to small three-lobed seed capsules that scatter and overwinter in the sand. It completes its entire life cycle in a single season, dying back after frost but reliably reseeding into the loose, well-drained, nutrient-poor sand it requires. Because it has almost no tolerance for shade, competition, or amended soil, it is best suited to a true sand garden or beach-adjacent planting rather than a conventional border.

planting.note: Direct sow into pure, infertile sandy soil in full sun in spring; jointweed germinates and grows quickly in loose sand but fails in fertile or moisture-retentive garden soil.

directions: Coastal jointweed is a slender, wiry-stemmed annual of open dune sand and sterile sandy barrens from Atlantic Canada and New England south along the coastal plain, named for the conspicuously swollen joints along its sparse, needle-like leaves and branching stems. In late summer and fall it produces airy, cloud-like sprays of tiny white to pink flowers that provide a late-season nectar source for small native bees and butterflies when little else is blooming on open sand. The plant is a true pioneer of disturbed, shifting, nutrient-poor sand and tolerates intense heat, drought, and exposure that exclude most other herbaceous plants. It reseeds freely in loose sand but does not persist where organic matter accumulates or where it faces competition from taller vegetation.

planting.note: Plant divisions or fall-sown seed in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade beneath redwoods or other conifers; seed benefits from a cold, moist winter stratification period outdoors.

directions: Pacific sanicle grows scattered through the dappled light of redwood, Douglas-fir, and mixed-evergreen forest understories along the Pacific Coast, forming mounded clumps of glossy, deeply lobed basal leaves. In spring it sends up branching stalks topped with small, greenish-yellow compound umbels of tiny flowers, followed by distinctive bur-like seed capsules covered in hooked bristles that cling to passing animals for dispersal. It tolerates the dry-summer, wet-winter rhythm typical of coastal California woodlands and often goes semi-dormant during the driest months, resuming growth with fall rains. A tough, adaptable groundlayer plant for a shaded native woodland garden, it combines well with ferns and other redwood-understory perennials and needs little attention once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions into loose, damp sand near the upper beach or foredune in full sun; this cold-adapted succulent establishes best in cool, maritime conditions and struggles in hot, humid inland sites.

directions: Seabeach sandwort forms low, spreading mats of fleshy, pale yellow-green, succulent leaves on the cobble and sand beaches of the North Atlantic, ranging from the Arctic south through New England and, locally, into the upper mid-Atlantic. Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers appear among the leaves in summer, followed by small fleshy capsules, and the thick, water-storing foliage allows the plant to withstand salt spray, sand burial, and periodic inundation by storm tides. Its deep, fleshy roots and rhizomes help stabilize loose upper-beach sand, making it an ecologically important though rarely cultivated pioneer species. It is best suited to a cool-summer coastal garden directly on sand rather than conventional inland planting beds, since it generally fails in hot, humid climates.
